title: “Molten Ring” Galaxy
caption: The "Molten Ring" lensed galaxy GAL-CLUS-022058s, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: "Molten Ring" Galaxy, GAL-CLUS-022058s, PKS 0218-387 · constellation Fornax
credit: Saurabh Jha (Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: A galaxy's light curves around a spherical companion, forming a partial ring. This is GAL-CLUS-022058s in Fornax, nicknamed the "Molten Ring" by astronomer Saurabh Jha, whose team first observed it with Hubble. When NASA released the picture in December 2020, it described it as one of the largest Einstein rings ever seen, and nearly complete.

The ring is produced by gravitational lensing. Gravity from a massive object between us and the far galaxy bends that galaxy's light, smearing and magnifying it. In this case the light is boosted by a factor of twenty, which effectively turned Hubble into the equivalent of a 48-meter telescope.

After the release, a team led by Anastasio Díaz-Sánchez, of Spain's Universidad Politécnica de Cartagena, used the image to measure the galaxy's distance. It sits at the peak era of star formation in the universe's history, when the brightest dusty galaxies formed stars a thousand times faster than our own. That may help explain how today's giant elliptical galaxies built up so quickly.
scale: The lensed galaxy is about 9.4 billion light-years away, according to NASA.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 took the image. NASA shows F555W in blue, F555W combined with F755W in green, and F775W combined with the infrared F160W in red.
understand.eye: The F160W filter records infrared light beyond human vision, and foreground gravity magnifies the galaxy's light by a factor of 20, making it far brighter than it would otherwise appear.

behind.people: See full credit: Saurabh Jha (Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey)
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Modelling the lens was essential to recovering the galaxy's true properties, and Hubble's sharp view let the team pick out four duplicated images of the galaxy and its clumps of stars. Albert Einstein first considered this kind of lensing in 1912, before building it into his general theory of relativity.
sources: NASA release: Hubble Snapshot of “Molten Ring” Galaxy Prompts New Research
alt: The curved arc of a distant galaxy wrapping around a spherical companion galaxy.
